Affiliation: chin-lun.fu@jpmchase.com , anagha.p.kulkarni@jpmorgan.com Affiliation: hong.ni@jpmchase.com , behrouz.madahian@jpmchase.com Abstract Personalized LLM assistants must recover sparse evidence from long conversation histories across queries of varying complexity. We introduce APDMem ( A gent-controlled P rogressive D isclosure Mem ory), a hierarchical long-term memory architecture that applies progressive disclosure to memory retrieval. Rather than relying on a flat memory store or fixed retrieval granularity, APDMem represents conversation history as four progressively detailed layers: thematic summaries, personalized key facts, turn-level evidence notes, and raw messages. At inference time, a controller applies progressive disclosure to the memory hierarchy: it first reads high-level summaries and drills into finer evidence only when needed. This creates an adaptive cost–fidelity trade-off: simple queries can terminate early, while complex temporal, multi-hop, or exact-evidence queries trigger deeper inspection. A note synthesizer converts retrieved evidence into a query-focused structure that consolidates facts, orders events, and flags contradictions before final answer generation. Experiments on LongMemEval show that APDMem achieves strong performance for long-context memory reasoning while accessing only 8% of the total conversations. 1 Introduction Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shown strong performance on complex, multi-step tasks. However, personalized agents must operate across long-term, multi-session interactions, where relevant information may be scattered across many past conversations Xu et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2025) ; Yu et al. (2026) . Such agents must remember user preferences, factual details, temporal sequences, and recurring themes over time Chhikara et al. (2025) ; Xu et al. (2025) ; Fang et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2026) ; Rasmussen et al. (2025) . Without effective memory, agents suffer from contextual amnesia: they may fail to recall prior facts, lose track of evolving goals, or overlook cross-session connections. Prior works on memory systems improve long-term recall by transforming conversation history into specialized representations: MemoryBank uses a structured memory store for personalized dialogue Zhong et al. (2024) ; MemGPT manages information via virtual context and external memory Packer et al. (2024) ; A-MEM builds interconnected, evolving memory networks Xu et al. (2025) ; and Zep constructs temporal, entity-centric memory graphs Rasmussen et al. (2025) . Other systems reduce cost through compression or consolidation: LightMem uses staged memory processing Fang et al. (2026) , while SimpleMem retrieves over compact semantic memories Liu et al. (2026) . While these designs reduce retrieval cost, they also introduce additional memory machinery and require committing conversational context to external memory stores, graph nodes, or other abstractions. We introduce APDMem ( A gent-controlled P rogressive D isclosure Mem ory), a hierarchical memory system for efficient context recall in personalized agents. APDMem treats long-term memory access as a query-adaptive disclosure problem rather than a one-shot retrieval problem. Inspired by progressive disclosure Nielsen (1993) , it exposes coarse information first and reveals finer evidence as needed. APDMem stores conversations as lightweight Markdown layers—thematic summaries ( L 0 L_{0} ), personalized key facts ( L 1 L_{1} ), turn-level evidence notes ( L 2 L_{2} ), raw messages ( L 3 L_{3} )—rather than converting them into a specialized database, graph, or compressed-only representation. Unlike existing systems that fix the retrieved representation in advance, APDMem only materializes thematic summaries at ingestion time while preserving raw messages underneath. At inference time, the Progressive Disclosure Controller expands on demand into finer details like personalized key facts, turn-level evidence notes, or raw messages. After sufficient evidence is collected, the controller drafts an answer. For final answer generation, Organized Notes Synthesizer structures the evidence retrieved by the controller along with the draft answer into organized notes. These notes consolidate relevant evidence, align it with the query and provide the answer generator with structured grounding context instead of raw retrieved snippets, reducing noise and improving answer accuracy. APDMem frames long-term memory retrieval as a query-adaptive disclosure problem: it must determine which conversations matter and how much detail to expose. Concretely, APDMem introduces two coupled dimensions: (1) hierarchical memory organization (coarse summaries linked to finer-grained evidence) and (2) progressive disclosure as an explicit architectural principle governing how that hierarchy is accessed. That is, the agent is designed to open only the minimum memory level required, exposing coarse views first and revealing finer evidence only when needed, with the disclosure depth controlled through tool-mediated interactions. Our primary contributions are: • Coarse-to-fine memory formulation. We introduce a Multi-Resolution Memory Substrate that preserves raw messages beneath progressively abstract memory layers. • Agent-controlled query-adaptive memory disclosure. We introduce a Progressive Disclosure Controller that decomposes queries, handles temporal constraints, and drills into deeper memory layers when needed. • Organized Notes for grounded generation. We introduce an Organized Notes Synthesizer that grounds retrieved evidence and the controller’s draft answer into structured notes. • LongMemEval validation. We show that APDMem achieves strong performance on LongMemEval Wu et al. (2025) while accessing only 8% of the conversations. 2 Related Work 2.1 Memory Representations for LLM Agents Personalized agents require persistent memory to maintain continuity across interactions Zhang et al. (2026) ; Xu et al. (2026) . Prior works frame this as a long-term memory problem: agents must retain user-specific facts and temporal context across sessions to avoid contextual amnesia Chhikara et al. (2025) ; Fang et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2026) . Memory systems differ mainly in how they represent past interactions. Profile- or fact-based methods store distilled user information Zhong et al. (2024) ; Chhikara et al. (2025) ; episodic systems retrieve prior interaction traces Packer et al. (2024) ; Xu et al. (2025) ; graph-based systems such as Zep organize temporal entity-relation memories Rasmussen et al. (2025) ; and compression-based systems such as LightMem and SimpleMem reduce cost through staged consolidation or compact semantic memories Fang et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2026) . These approaches often require graph conversion, compression, or specialized memory objects, creating trade-offs between efficiency, fidelity, and complexity. APDMem instead stores conversations as transparent Markdown layers preserving the original conversation while providing compact abstractions for retrieval. Figure 1: APDMem overview. The Multi-Resolution Memory Substrate stores conversations as layered views from thematic summaries ( L 0 L_{0} ) to raw messages ( L 3 L_{3} ). The Progressive Disclosure Controller uses tool calls to retrieve and drill down only as needed. The Organized Notes Synthesizer then consolidates collected evidence into structured notes for grounded answer generation. The upper-right panel summarizes tools available to the controller. 2.2 Progressive Disclosure Memory systems organize information at different granularities—such as summaries, passages, chunks, or episodic traces—to improve retrieval over large contexts Sarthi et al. (2024) ; Gao et al. (2023) ; Izacard and Grave (2021) ; Khattab and Zaharia (2020) ; Lewis et al. (2020) ; Asai et al. (2024) ; Trivedi et al. (2023) . APDMem builds on this idea through progressive disclosure Nielsen (1993) , exposing coarse memory views first and revealing finer evidence only when needed. To our knowledge, APDMem is the first system to make progressive disclosure an explicit architectural principle for agent memory, with an agent controlling disclosure depth through tool-mediated interactions. 2.3 Evidence-Grounded Generation Complex queries involving temporal constraints, ambiguous references, user-specific details, multi-hop reasoning, or enumeration often require iterative retrieval and verification Yao et al. (2023) ; Schick et al. (2023) ; Press et al. (2023) ; Trivedi et al. (2023) . Prior work has shown the value of organizing or reasoning over retrieved evidence before answer generation Yu et al. (2024) ; Gao et al. (2023) ; Asai et al. (2024) . Inspired by Chain-of-Note Yu et al. (2024) , APDMem converts retrieved evidence into organized notes that consolidate relevant facts, temporal order, contradictions, enumeration evidence, and answer hints into a structured grounding context for the answer generator. 3 APDMem As shown in Figure 1 , APDMem consists of three components: (1) a Multi-Resolution Memory Substrate that stores each conversation across four layers of increasing abstraction (§ 3.1 ); (2) a Progressive Disclosure Controller that searches, drills into, and reflects over the memory hierarchy through tool-mediated interactions (§ 3.2 ); and (3) an Organized Notes Synthesizer that structures retrieved evidence for final answer generation (§ 3.3 ). 3.1 Multi-Resolution Memory Substrate Given a conversation history, we partition it into N N sessions 𝒮 = S 1 , … , S N \mathcal{S}={S_{1},\ldots,S_{N}} , where each session S i S_{i} is a contiguous conversation episode consisting of turns, and each turn is a user–assistant exchange. APDMem represents each session as a four-layer memory tuple, S i = ( L 0 , L 1 , L 2 , L 3 ) S_{i}=(L_{0},L_{1},L_{2},L_{3}) . L 0 L_{0} contains thematic summaries with resolved pronouns, normalized dates, keywords, and tags, and serves as the primary indexing layer. L 1 L_{1} contains personalized key facts : session facts about user information, recommendations, plans, preferences, and constraints. L 2 L_{2} contains turn-level evidence notes : turn-level factual bullets that preserve temporal order for fine-grained evidence reasoning. L 3 L_{3} contains raw messages : the verbatim user--assistant messages retained for exact evidence recovery. 1 1 1 Construction details, prompts, and real output examples for each layer are provided in Appendix I . Lazy materialization. Only L 0 L_{0} and L 3 L_{3} are materialized at ingestion time, whereas L 1 L_{1} and L 2 L_{2} are generated on demand when first requested by the progressive disclosure controller and then cached for reuse, reducing write-time cost. 3.2 Progressive Disclosure Controller The Progressive Disclosure Controller implements memory access as a bounded, query-adaptive control process. Given a query q q , the controller’s objective is to gather sufficient evidence for answering q q while avoiding unnecessary disclosure of finer memory. It maintains an evidence set 𝒱 t \mathcal{V}_{t} at step t t . Each element in 𝒱 \mathcal{V} is a retrieved view of a session S i S_{i} at abstraction level L ℓ L_{\ell} for ℓ ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 } \ell\in\{0,1,2,3\} . At each step, the controller selects a tool action a t ∈ 𝒜 a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} , where 𝒜 = { search , read_facts , read_turns , read_raw , interpret_dates , decompose , reflect } \mathcal{A}=\{\texttt{search},\texttt{read\_facts},\\ \texttt{read\_turns},\texttt{read\_raw},\texttt{interpret\_dates},\\ \texttt{decompose},\texttt{reflect}\} is the action space. Memory-read actions correspond to different resolutions of the Multi-Resolution Memory Substrate : finer layers expose higher-fidelity evidence but incur greater token and latency cost, i.e., c ⁡ ( L 0 ) < c ⁡ ( L 1 ) < c ⁡ ( L 2 ) < c ⁡ ( L 3 ) c(L_{0})<c(L_{1})<c(L_{2})<c(L_{3}) and f ⁡ ( L 0 ) < f ⁡ ( L 1 ) < f ⁡ ( L 2 ) < f ⁡ ( L 3 ) f(L_{0})<f(L_{1})<f(L_{2})<f(L_{3}) , where c ⁡ ( ⋅ ) c(\cdot) denotes access cost and f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) f(\cdot) denotes evidence fidelity. The highest value in each column is shown in bold ; the second highest is underlined . 3.2.1 Controller Workflow A typical trajectory proceeds in three phases. Query preparation. Queries with relative dates (e.g., “last summer”) are normalized against the question timestamp via interpret_dates ; multi-hop or compound queries are split into focused subqueries via decompose . Progressive disclosure. search retrieves the top- K K candidate sessions over L 0 L_{0} (hybrid lexical + dense retrieval fused with RRF; Appendix G ). An auto-drill step selects the most promising unexplored sessions and read_facts retrieves their L 1 L_{1} key facts. If these facts are insufficient, the controller descends further: read_turns surfaces L 2 L_{2} evidence in temporal order, and read_raw retrieves L 3 L_{3} messages restricted to the most relevant turns within selected sessions. At each step, retrieved session information is stored in evidence set 𝒱 \mathcal{V} . Reflection and drafting. APDMem uses reflection Yao et al. (2023) ; Shinn et al. (2023) to avoid both premature answering and unbounded search. reflect summarizes 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , identifies missing evidence, and assesses whether additional retrieval is likely to help. If more evidence is needed, it proposes follow-up queries and the controller re-enters the progressive disclosure phase. Once 𝒱 \mathcal{V} converges (§ 3.2.2 ), the controller produces a draft answer a draft a_{\text{draft}} from the final evidence set 𝒱 T \mathcal{V}_{T} , which is then passed to the Organized Notes Synthesizer. 3.2.2 Convergence Control The controller loop terminates when (1) reflection finds no new evidence, | 𝒱 t | = | 𝒱 t − 1 | |\mathcal{V}_{t}|=|\mathcal{V}_{t-1}| , or (2) step budget T max T_{\max} is reached. T max T_{\max} caps the maximum number of controller iterations and therefore bounds the additional tool calls the controller can make before it must stop escalating and return the best available answer. 2 2 2 In all experiments, we set T max = 20 T_{\max}=20 . Appendix D reports the observed iteration distribution and discusses how to choose T max T_{\max} for other applications. 3.3 Organized Notes Synthesizer The Organized Notes Synthesizer converts the query q q , evidence set 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , and controller’s draft answer a draft a_{\text{draft}} into organized notes, a compact intermediate representation. Inspired by Chain-of-Note Yu et al. (2024) , this step uses the draft to verify, correct, or supplement the controller’s initial reasoning. These notes organize relevant facts, temporal ordering, contradictions, enumeration evidence for counting queries, and an answer hint into a query-focused grounding context. Answer generation. The answer generator receives the organized notes and a draft a_{\text{draft}} to produce the final response. This synthesize-then-generate design preserves the controller’s retrieval trajectory while allowing the final answer to correct errors or omissions surfaced during evidence synthesis. 4 Experiments Experimental Setup. We evaluate on LongMemEval Wu et al. (2025) (specifically the LongMemEval-S split): 500 questions across six categories (Table 1 column headers), each paired with a per-question session haystack. We compare against Full-context (no retrieval), Mem0 Chhikara et al. (2025) , LightMem Fang et al. (2026) , and SimpleMem Liu et al. (2026) . APDMem and each baseline are evaluated with GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.1-mini as backbones; for APDMem, a single backbone drives the Progressive Disclosure Controller , and the Organized Notes Synthesizer . 4 4 4 Full implementation details and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix B , C , and G . 4.1 Main Experiments Table 1 presents the main results. APDMem reaches 87.8% with GPT-4.1 and 79.8% with GPT-4.1-mini, ahead of the best prior baseline (SimpleMem) by 3.8 and 2.9 points respectively. The gains are clearest on detail-oriented queries. For example, on SS-Asst, APDMem reaches 100.0% with GPT-4.1, surpassing SimpleMem (76.8%) and Full-context (96.4%) while inspecting only a small slice of the haystack (§ 4.3 ). This highlights the value of drilling to raw turns. APDMem remains strong on multi-session synthesis with GPT-4.1, scoring 77.4%, though SimpleMem is higher at 81.2%. This reflects a breadth-depth trade-off: flat summary retrieval can expose more sessions per call, while APDMem investigates top-ranked candidates in greater detail. Notably, this is not a systematic weakness: with GPT-4.1-mini, APDMem achieves the best multi-session score, showing that targeted memory navigation can also benefit multi-session reasoning. 4.2 Inference Efficiency We decompose cost into offline (one-time L 0 L_{0} construction) and online (per-query controller cost, including on-demand L 1 L_{1} / L 2 L_{2} generation).
